vulnerability.title: Ensure auditd Collects Changes to Cron Jobs - /etc/cron.d/
vulnerability.description: At a minimum, the audit system should collect administrator actions for all users and root. If the auditd daemon is configured to use the augenrules program to read audit rules during daemon startup (the default), add the following lines to a file with suffix .rules in the directory /etc/audit/rules.d: -w /etc/cron.d/ -p wa -k cronjobs If the auditd daemon is configured to use the auditctl utility to read audit rules during daemon startup, add the following lines to /etc/audit/audit.rules: -w /etc/cron.d/ -p wa -k cronjobs
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q audit && rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then # Perform the remediation for both possible tools: 'auditctl' and 'augenrules' # Create a list of audit *.rules files that should be inspected for presence and correctness # of a particular audit rule. The scheme is as follows: # # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Tool used to load audit rules | Rule already defined | Audit rules file to inspect | # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # auditctl | Doesn't matter | /etc/audit/audit.rules | # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # augenrules | Yes | /etc/audit/rules.

triage_decision.reason: Adding an audit rule for /etc/cron.d/ is a standard configuration change that does not affect authentication, networking, or filesystem integrity, and it follows STIG hardening patterns for auditd.

review_feedback: The plan falls short because it does not reload or restart auditd after modifying the rules, so the new audit rule will not be active until a service restart. Furthermore, overwriting an existing /etc/audit/rules.d/cronjobs.rules file may unintentionally strip other rules that were already present in that file. The script also does not explicitly set ownership on the new file, which could lead to unintended permissions if the script runs with unexpected UID/GID.

concerns: Missing reload/restart of auditd after rule change
Overwrites existing cronjobs.rules content potentially deleting other rules
No explicit ownership/permission enforcement beyond the mode
suggested_improvements: After modifying /etc/audit/rules.d/cronjobs.rules or /etc/audit/audit.rules, run `systemctl reload auditd` or `auditctl -R` to apply changes.
Prefer appending the rule to /etc/audit/rules.d/cronjobs.rules if the file exists rather than overwriting it, or at least preserve existing content.
Set file ownership to root:root after creation to ensure correct permissions.
